title: Annotatio I §.IV: Replies (1)–(2) — complexum unproven; Luther vs King of England on hoc = bread
pass_a_gloss: For I reply (1) that the Complex has not yet been proved, (2) that the Complex is disapproved by Luther, who lays down that by the pronoun this nothing other than bread is to be understood — then in the book against the King of England, where he says: From the thread of the speech I have shown that the pronoun this is fitted to the bread and so the open words sound: This is my body i.e. this bread is my body: For the Text so has: he took bread &c. You see here that all those words — he took, blessed, broke &c. — are said of the bread, and the same the pronoun this demonstrates, because that very thing which He blessed, broke and gave — this, I say, received, blessed and broken — is signified when it is said: this is my body. Not the predicate but the subject is demonstrated. For He did not take, bless and break His body, but bread. &c. These are clear words which the wicked King hid and presses that naked proposition This is my body, and fits the pronoun this properly and immediately to the body.
pass_b_english: Reply (1): the Complex is not yet proved.
Reply (2): Luther himself rejects it — hoc means nothing but bread.

Against the King of England he threads the Institution verbs (took, blessed, broke) onto the bread: This is my body = this bread is my body; the pronoun shows the subject, not the predicate — the King hid those clear words and pressed the naked proposition onto the body.
source_text: Nam respondeo (1) Complexum nondum probatum esse, (2) Complexum Luthero improbari, per pronomen hoc nihil aliud quam panem intelligendum edicenti, tùm in libro contra Regem Angliae, ubi ait: Ex filo sermonis ostendi, pronomen hoc ad panem aptari & sic sonare aperta verba: Hoc est corpus meum i. e. hic panis est corpus meum: Nam Textus sic habet: accepit panem &c. vides hic quòd omnia illa verba: accepit, benedixit, fregit &c. de pane dicantur, & eundem demonstrat pronomen hoc, quia id ipsum quod benedixit, fregit & dedit, hoc inquam acceptum benedictum & fractum significatur, cum dicitur: hoc est corpus meum. Non praedicatum, sed subjectum demonstratur. Non enim corpus suum accepit, benedixit & fregit, sed panem. &c. hae sunt clara verba quae Rex nequitiosus occulit & nudam illam propositionem urget: Hoc est corpus meum, & pronomen hoc ad corpus propriè & immediatè aptat.

rejected: the subject is demonstrated in court only
